title: Units & Values
summary: **CSS units** describe how big things are. Absolute units like `px` are fixed, while relative units like `em`, `rem`, `%`, and viewport units (`vw`/`vh`) scale with context — choosing the right one is the key to responsive, accessible layouts.

subtopics.title: Absolute units (px)
subtopics.explanation: Absolute units have a fixed size regardless of context. px is by far the most common — one CSS pixel is a device-independent unit that stays consistent. Other absolute units (pt, cm, in) are mainly for print. px is great for borders, fine details, and small fixed offsets, but using px for font sizes ignores the user's browser font preference.

subtopics.title: rem — relative to the root
subtopics.explanation: 1rem equals the root (html) font size, which is 16px by default. Because every rem references the same root, sizing is predictable and scales globally when a user changes their browser font size. rem is the recommended unit for font sizes, spacing, and most layout dimensions in accessible, responsive designs.

subtopics.title: em — relative to the element
subtopics.explanation: 1em equals the current element's font size, so em is contextual and compounds when nested (an em inside an em inside an em multiplies). em is excellent for sizing things relative to their OWN text — like padding on a button that should grow with its font — but can cause surprises in deeply nested structures.
subtopics.example:
.btn { font-size: 1rem; padding: 0.5em 1em; }
/* padding scales with the button's font size */

subtopics.title: Percentages (%)
subtopics.explanation: Percentages are relative to a parent's corresponding dimension: width: 50% is half the parent's width; for padding/margin, percentages are relative to the parent's WIDTH (even vertically), which trips people up. Percentages are the basis of fluid layouts that resize with their container.
subtopics.example:
width: 50%;        /* half the parent's width */
max-width: 100%;   /* never overflow the parent */

subtopics.title: Viewport units (vw, vh)
subtopics.explanation: 1vw is 1% of the viewport width and 1vh is 1% of the viewport height, so they scale with the browser window itself. height: 100vh makes a full-screen section; vw is handy for large fluid hero text. Beware that 100vw can include the scrollbar width, and mobile address bars affect vh (newer units like dvh address this).
subtopics.example:
min-height: 100vh; /* full viewport height */
font-size: 5vw;    /* scales with window width */

subtopics.title: ch and other text-relative units
subtopics.explanation: 1ch is roughly the width of the '0' character in the current font, making it ideal for limiting line length for readability (around 60ch is comfortable for body text). Related units like ex exist but are rarely used; ch is the practical one for typographic measure.

subtopics.title: Unitless line-height
subtopics.explanation: line-height should almost always be unitless (e.g. 1.5). A unitless value is a multiplier of the element's own font size and is inherited as the RATIO, so children compute their own correct line height. Using line-height: 1.5em or a px value passes down a fixed computed value that can break for differently sized children.
subtopics.example: body { line-height: 1.5; } /* 1.5x each element's font size */

subtopics.title: Keyword values like auto
subtopics.explanation: Not all values are numbers. Keywords carry meaning: width: auto lets a block fill available space, margin: auto centers (or absorbs free space in flex), and height: auto sizes to content. Other keywords (inherit, initial, unset, currentColor) control how values are resolved. Knowing keywords avoids hard-coding numbers the browser can compute better.
subtopics.example:
margin: 0 auto; /* auto absorbs free space -> centered */
width: auto;    /* fill available inline space */

foundations.overview: Every CSS value carries a unit (or a keyword) that tells the browser how to interpret a number. The crucial distinction is absolute (fixed, like px) versus relative (scales with context, like rem, em, %, vw/vh). Choosing relative units where they matter is what makes interfaces responsive and accessible rather than brittle.
foundations.formalDefinition: CSS units are the dimension types appended to numeric values; absolute units have a fixed physical/pixel size, while relative units compute their value from a reference such as the root font size, the parent, the element, or the viewport.
foundations.whyItMatters: Unit choice determines whether your UI respects user font-size preferences, adapts to screen size, and stays readable — directly affecting accessibility and responsiveness.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of px as a ruler that never changes, rem as a ruler tied to a single master dial (the root font size), em as a ruler that resizes per element, and vw/vh as rulers stretched across the window.
foundations.browserPerspective: When the browser computes styles, it resolves every relative unit to absolute pixels using the relevant reference (root size for rem, element size for em, parent size for %, viewport size for vw/vh) before layout and paint.
foundations.realWorldUsage: rem for typography and spacing, em for component-internal padding, % for fluid widths, vh for full-height sections, and ch for readable text columns are the everyday combinations in production design systems.
foundations.businessImpact: Layouts that scale with user settings and screen sizes reach more users (including those who increase font size for readability), improving accessibility compliance and engagement.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A consistent unit strategy (e.g. rem-based spacing scale) reduces magic numbers and makes responsive behavior predictable and easy to adjust globally.
foundations.performanceImpact: Units themselves don't affect performance meaningfully, but viewport units that change on scroll (mobile vh) can cause layout shifts; choosing stable units avoids jank.
commonUseCases: rem for font sizes and a global spacing scale
% and max-width for fluid, capped containers
vh for full-screen sections and vw for fluid hero text
ch to constrain readable line length

commonMisconceptions.myth: px and rem are interchangeable for font sizes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: px ignores the user's browser font-size setting; rem scales with it, which matters for accessibility.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Percentage vertical padding is relative to height.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Percentage padding and margin are always relative to the parent's WIDTH, even top/bottom values.

commonMisconceptions.myth: line-height should use em or px for precision.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unitless line-height is preferred because it inherits as a ratio, so each element computes the correct height for its own font size.

visualExplorer.title: How units resolve
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how the browser turns each relative unit into pixels using its reference value.

steps.title: px (absolute)
steps.description: A fixed size. 16px is always 16px regardless of context — used for borders and fine details.

steps.title: rem (root-relative)
steps.description: Multiplied by the root font size. With root 16px, 1.5rem resolves to 24px and scales globally if the root changes.

steps.title: em (element-relative)
steps.description: Multiplied by the element's own font size; compounds when nested, so 1.2em inside 1.2em grows quickly.

steps.title: % (parent-relative)
steps.description: A fraction of the parent's dimension; width: 50% is half the parent, and % padding references the parent's width.

steps.title: vw / vh (viewport-relative)
steps.description: 1% of the viewport width or height; 100vh fills the screen and 5vw scales text with window width.

debuggingLab.title: Why are nested labels getting huge?
debuggingLab.symptom: Each nested .tag is bigger than its parent, growing out of control the deeper they nest.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: em is relative to the element's own (inherited) font size, so it COMPOUNDS when elements nest: 1.4em x 1.4em x 1.4em makes level 3 about 2.7x the base size. The text balloons with depth.
commonMistakes: Assuming em is relative to the root like rem.
Using em for font sizes inside recursively nested structures.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Switch the font size to a unit that references the root instead of the parent.

theory.question: What is the difference between absolute and relative units in CSS? Give examples.
theory.directAnswer: Absolute units have a fixed size regardless of context — px is the main one (also pt, cm, in for print). Relative units compute their size from a reference: rem from the root font size, em from the element's own font size, % from the parent, and vw/vh from the viewport. Relative units are what make layouts responsive and accessible.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two families of length values: fixed (absolute) and context-dependent (relative).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Fixed units give precise control for details; relative units let UIs adapt to user settings and screen sizes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser resolves relative units to pixels at compute time using the appropriate reference (root, element, parent, or viewport).

theory.whyImportant: Choosing units correctly is central to responsive design and accessibility, and it's a common fundamentals question.
theory.realWorldExample: A design system uses rem for type and spacing so the whole UI scales when a user increases their browser font size.

nestedTopics.title: px
nestedTopics.explanation: Fixed; good for borders and fine details, weak for font sizing accessibility.

nestedTopics.title: rem vs em
nestedTopics.explanation: rem references the root (no compounding); em references the element (compounds when nested).

nestedTopics.title: viewport units
nestedTopics.explanation: vw/vh scale with the window, enabling full-screen and fluid sizing.

followUps.question: Why prefer rem over px for font sizes?
followUps.answer: rem scales with the user's browser font-size preference, respecting accessibility; px ignores it.

followUps.question: What is the reference for percentage padding?
followUps.answer: Always the parent's width, even for top and bottom padding/margin.

theory.question: Why is a unitless line-height recommended over em or px?
theory.directAnswer: A unitless line-height is a multiplier of each element's own font size and is inherited as that RATIO, so every descendant computes a correct line height for its size. With line-height: 1.5em or a px value, a single computed length is inherited, which can be too tight or too loose for children whose font sizes differ.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: line-height set as a bare number, e.g. 1.5, with no unit.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make line spacing scale proportionally with text size throughout the tree.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Unitless values inherit the factor and are recomputed per element; unit values inherit the already-computed length.

theory.whyImportant: It prevents subtle, hard-to-debug spacing problems in nested text and is a classic 'gotcha' question.
theory.realWorldExample: Setting body { line-height: 1.5 } gives headings and small print each appropriately proportional spacing automatically.

nestedTopics.title: Inheriting a ratio
nestedTopics.explanation: Each element multiplies the ratio by its own font size.

nestedTopics.title: The em pitfall
nestedTopics.explanation: line-height: 1.5em inherits a fixed length that may not suit children.

followUps.question: What's a sensible default body line-height?
followUps.answer: Around 1.4-1.6 for body text; tighter (closer to 1.1-1.2) for large headings.

scenario.question: A teammate hard-codes all font sizes and spacing in px. An accessibility audit fails because text doesn't scale when users change their browser font size. How do you reason about and fix this?
scenario.directAnswer: px is absolute, so it ignores the user's root font-size preference; that's why text won't scale. The fix is to base typography and spacing on rem, which references the root font size. Set a sensible html font size (or leave the default 16px), then express sizes in rem so increasing the browser font scales the whole UI proportionally.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An accessibility issue caused by absolute units ignoring user preferences.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: px is fixed by definition; only root-relative units respond to the user's font setting.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Switching to rem ties sizes to the root, so a larger root from user settings scales everything.

scenario.whyImportant: Respecting user font-size settings is an accessibility requirement and a real-world correctness issue.

nestedTopics.title: rem for type
nestedTopics.explanation: Express font sizes in rem so they track the root size.

nestedTopics.title: Keep px for borders
nestedTopics.explanation: Hairline borders and tiny details can stay px without harming accessibility.

followUps.question: Should you set html { font-size: 62.5% }?
followUps.answer: It makes 1rem = 10px for easy math, but it can interfere with the user's chosen base size; many teams just keep the default 16px and use rem directly.

coding.question: Write CSS for a responsive section that is at least full screen height, has a readable text column, and uses accessible relative units throughout.
coding.thoughtProcess: Use min-height: 100vh so the section fills the viewport but can grow with content. Use rem for spacing and font size for accessibility, a unitless line-height so it scales per element, and a ch-based max-width to cap line length for readability. Center the text column horizontally.
coding.lineByLine: min-height: 100vh fills the screen but allows growth. padding/font-size in rem scale with the root for accessibility. line-height: 1.6 is unitless so it inherits as a ratio. .prose uses max-width: 60ch to cap line length for readability and margin: 0 auto to center the column.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use dvh for mobile
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Swap 100vh for 100dvh so mobile browser chrome (address bar) doesn't cause the section to jump.

followUps.question: Why min-height: 100vh instead of height: 100vh?
followUps.answer: height: 100vh clips or overflows when content exceeds the viewport; min-height lets the section grow with its content while still filling the screen as a minimum.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Production design systems standardize on rem for typography and a rem-based spacing scale, reserving px for hairline borders and fine details. Percentages and viewport units handle fluid widths and full-screen sections, while ch constrains readable text columns — a small, deliberate palette of units rather than ad-hoc mixing.
productionDeepDive.performance: Units rarely affect performance, but viewport units tied to mobile chrome (vh) can trigger layout shifts on scroll; newer dynamic viewport units (dvh/svh/lvh) reduce that jank. Avoid animating layout-affecting units; prefer transforms.
productionDeepDive.security: Units have no security surface, but uncontrolled relative sizing of user content can break layouts; pair fluid units with max-width and overflow controls to keep content bounded.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Define a tokenized spacing scale in rem (0.25/0.5/1/1.5/2rem) and a type scale so dozens of components stay consistent and globally adjustable by changing the root or tokens.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer rem and unitless line-height to avoid compounding and inheritance surprises; document when px is acceptable (borders, shadows) so the codebase stays consistent.
productionDeepDive.observability: Browser DevTools shows computed pixel values for any relative unit, letting you verify how rem/em/%/vw resolve in context when debugging unexpected sizes.

caseStudies.problem: px-based typography ignored user font-size settings and failed audits.
caseStudies.solution: Migrated type and spacing to a rem-based scale tied to the root font size.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires discipline to avoid mixing units; some pixel math becomes less obvious.
caseStudies.lessons: A rem-first unit strategy makes UIs both responsive and accessible by default.

keyTakeaways: Absolute units (px) are fixed; relative units (rem, em, %, vw/vh, ch) scale with a reference and enable responsive, accessible design.
rem references the root font size (predictable, no compounding); em references the element's own size and compounds when nested.
Percentages are relative to the parent's dimension — and % padding/margin is always relative to the parent's WIDTH.
Viewport units (vw/vh) scale with the window; use min-height: 100vh (or dvh on mobile) for full-screen sections.
Use unitless line-height (e.g. 1.5) so it inherits as a ratio, and ch to cap text at a readable line length.
